sbh3.1:0.2: The Nine Stages of Mental Abiding
sbh3.1:1.1: One-pointedness (*ekāgratā*) has both the side of śamatha (calm-abiding) and the side of vipaśyanā (insight).
sbh3.1:1.2: The one-pointedness in the nine-fold continuity or abiding of mind belongs to the śamatha side; the one-pointedness in the four-fold support of wisdom belongs to the vipaśyanā side.
sbh3.1:2.1: What is the nine-fold mental abiding?
sbh3.1:2.2: Here a monk places (*sthāpayati*) the mind inwardly,
sbh3.1:2.4: places it again (*avasthāpayati*), places it closely (*upasthāpayati*),
sbh3.1:3.2: Withdrawing it from all outer objects, he ties it inwardly toward non-distraction.
sbh3.1:3.3: That first binding [of the mind] against distraction — this is placement.
sbh3.1:4.1: How does he place it continuously?
sbh3.1:4.2: That mind first bound is [Conjectural: unsteady], gross, unsettled, and not fully settled. On that very same object, through the practice of strengthening and the practice of clarification, with deliberate restraint — making it subtle and gathering it together — he places it continuously.
sbh3.1:5.1: How does he place it again?
sbh3.1:5.2: If, while he is placing the mind,
sbh3.1:5.3: it becomes distracted outwardly through loss of mindfulness, [Lacuna]
sbh3.1:6.2: By those signs which distract his mind —
sbh3.1:6.3: namely the signs of [Conjectural: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles], and the signs of passion, hatred, delusion, and of women and men —
sbh3.1:6.4: with regard to these, he has previously grasped the perception of danger;
sbh3.1:6.5: taking that as governing, he does not allow the mind to spread out toward those signs.
sbh3.1:7.2: By those thoughts — sensual thoughts and the like —
sbh3.1:7.4: the hindrance of sensual desire and the like —
sbh3.1:7.5: there is agitation of the mind.
sbh3.1:7.6: With regard to these, he has previously grasped the perception of danger;
sbh3.1:7.8: toward those thoughts and secondary defilements
sbh3.1:7.9: he does not allow [the mind] to spread out — thus he pacifies it.
sbh3.1:8.2: When, through loss of mindfulness, both of these become active, he does not tolerate the thoughts and secondary defilements as they arise, one after another;
sbh3.1:9.1: How does he make [the mind] single-pointed?
sbh3.1:9.2: With effort, he establishes an unbroken, uninterrupted flow of samādhi — thus he makes it single-pointed.
sbh3.1:10.2: Through familiarization, cultivation, and frequent practice, a path proceeding effortlessly,
sbh3.1:10.5: by which, without effort, without exertion, the flow of his mind's samādhi
sbh3.1:11.1: The nine-fold mental abiding is accomplished through the six kinds of power —
sbh3.1:11.2: namely the powers of hearing and thinking (*śruta-cintā-bala*), the power of mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*) [Conjectural: and the power of clear comprehension], the power of diligence (*vīrya-bala*), and the power of familiarity (*paricaya-bala*).
sbh3.1:12.1: First, through the powers of hearing and thinking:
sbh3.1:12.2: taking what he has heard and what he has reflected on as governing, from the very beginning he places the mind on the object;
sbh3.1:12.4: by sustained engagement, he places it continuously.
sbh3.1:12.5: Returning [to it] through the power of mindfulness, he places again the mind bound there
sbh3.1:12.7: Then through the power of clear comprehension (*saṁprajanya-bala*), not allowing the mind to spread toward distracting signs, thoughts, and secondary defilements, he tames
sbh3.1:12.10: he does not tolerate the occurrence of both of these; [Conjectural: he fully pacifies]
sbh3.1:12.12: Through the power of familiarity, he concentrates.
sbh3.1:13.1: In the nine-fold mental abiding, four [kinds of] attention should be known:
sbh3.1:13.2: forceful attention, interrupted attention, uninterrupted attention, and effortless attention.
sbh3.1:14.1: In one who is placing and placing continuously, the attention is forceful (*bala-vāhana*).
sbh3.1:14.2: In one who is placing again, placing closely, taming, pacifying, or fully pacifying, the attention is interrupted (*sacchidra-vāhana*).
sbh3.1:14.3: In one who is making single-pointed, the attention is uninterrupted (*niścchidra-vāhana*).
sbh3.1:14.4: In one who is concentrating, the attention is effortless (*anābhoga-vāhana*).
sbh3.1:15.1: Thus these [four] attentions in mental abiding belong to the śamatha side.
sbh3.1:15.2: But for one who, having thus attained inward calm of mind, applies himself to vipaśyanā —
sbh3.1:15.3: for him these very same four attentions belong to the vipaśyanā side.
